sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
October 2026 delivered a stark bifurcation across global equity markets, as a sharp AI-spending recalibration in US mega-cap technology contrasted with resilience in defensive sectors, energy, and select European markets. The Nasdaq Composite recorded its worst monthly decline since March 2025, shedding **5.28%**, while the more cyclically balanced Dow Jones Industrial Average bucked the selloff to gain **1.76%**. The S&P 500 navigated the crosscurrents to finish marginally lower, registering a decline of **0.87%** to an estimated close near **7,585** (approx., verify before merging).

European indices demonstrated relative resilience amid the US tech tumult, with London's FTSE 100 posting its first monthly gain in three consecutive months. APAC markets were more volatile: the Shanghai Composite plumbed 52-week closing lows as China's AI hardware complex sold off aggressively, while the Hang Seng benefited from rotation out of mainland equities. Oil-producing and financial-sector heavyweights provided an offsetting tailwind across multiple geographies, lifted by Brent's sharp monthly surge toward **$118/bbl**.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
AI CapEx Reality Check -- Alphabet's Q3 2026 results, reported on October 28, delivered the most consequential single-name catalyst of the month. The company posted its first top-and-bottom-line miss in nearly four years: revenue grew **25%** year-on-year but fell short of consensus, GAAP EPS came in at **$2.12** versus **$2.87** in the prior year, and quarterly capex reached **$51.36 billion**, stoking deep concern over return-on-investment timelines for the AI buildout.

The most alarming figure was free cash flow of negative **$9.07 billion** in Q3 — far worse than the negative **$2.70 billion** analysts had modelled — marking the second consecutive quarter of negative FCF. Full-year 2026 capex guidance was held at **$195–205 billion**, while management signalled 2027 outlays would increase significantly, with sell-side projections coalescing around **$300 billion**. Alphabet shares fell more than **12%** in the sessions following the report, dragging the Nasdaq technology complex lower and triggering a broader reassessment of the AI mega-cycle's near-term cash economics.

Google Cloud revenue nearly doubled, rising **+103%** to **$30.7 billion**, demonstrating robust demand — but the cash-burn trajectory shifted the investment debate from AI revenue potential to its fiscal sustainability. The rout extended to Intel and other AI-infrastructure names, cementing October as the month the market began pricing execution risk into the generational spending wave.

Fed Hawkish Hold & Treasury Yield Surge -- The Federal Open Market Committee voted 10 to 2 to hold the federal funds rate target at **3.75%–4.00%** at its October 28 meeting, with two members dissenting in favour of an immediate rate increase. The hawkish undertone reignited the "higher for longer" narrative that had unsettled risk assets in prior quarters and drove a fresh leg higher in US Treasury yields across the curve.

The 10-year Treasury yield peaked near **5.13%** in mid-October — its highest level of 2026 — before retracing modestly to approximately **4.94%** by month end (approx., verify before merging). The 2-year yield reached **4.81%** at the intra-month peak before settling near **4.69%** by October 23. Notably, October 22 delivered the strongest single-session Treasury rally in over a year, as a brief flight-to-quality impulse pulled the 10-year sharply lower intraday before yields resumed their upward trajectory.

The combination of elevated real yields and a firmer US dollar was the principal headwind for gold, which slid to a one-year low, losing approximately **6.5%** over the month. The DXY dollar index firmed to close near **102** (approx., verify before merging), reflecting the yield differential advantage the Fed's hawkish posture conferred on the greenback and pressuring both EM and G10 currencies broadly.

Strait of Hormuz Supply Shock -- Escalating attacks on tanker shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, running at near-record levels according to UKMTO incident reports, drove Brent crude to a six-month high near **$118/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) in late October, contributing to a monthly gain of approximately **14%** for the benchmark. The pre-conflict strait facilitates roughly one-fifth of global seaborne oil supply, and the sustained chokepoint risk embedded a substantial geopolitical premium across energy markets throughout the month.

Geopolitical positioning amplified the market reaction: President Trump publicly threatened renewed military strikes on Iran's oil infrastructure following the US midterm elections, while reports indicated Israeli leadership was pressing for joint action. These signals extended the rally well beyond what supply disruption alone might have justified, with Brent's premium over WTI widening materially as logistics constraints penalised Atlantic Basin crudes less than Gulf producers. WTI crude settled near **$104/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) by October 30.

The oil surge had meaningful second-order effects: energy equities outperformed sharply across the S&P 500 and FTSE 100, inflation breakevens ticked higher at the margin, and central bank communication became more guarded about the pace of any future easing cycle, reinforcing the Fed's hawkish hold narrative and suppressing rate-cut expectations heading into year end.

Global Sector Rotation: Defensives Dominate -- October crystallised one of the most pronounced sector rotation episodes of 2026. Within the S&P 500, the technology sector (XLK) fell **8.3%** as Alphabet's earnings sparked contagion across AI-exposed names, while healthcare, financials, consumer staples, and energy all posted positive returns that together kept the index close to flat. The Dow Jones Industrial Average's **+1.76%** gain against the Nasdaq's **-5.28%** loss represented the widest monthly divergence between the two benchmarks in 2026.

The rotation extended beyond US borders. In the UK, the FTSE 100 rose approximately **+1%** to close near **10,730** (approx., verify before merging), recording its first monthly advance in three consecutive months, partly reflecting its structurally higher weighting in energy and financial stocks. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng closed near **23,294** (approx., verify before merging), supported by investor rotation away from mainland Chinese technology and into consumer, logistics, and banking names.

Q3 S&P 500 earnings season provided a constructive underpinning: blended year-on-year earnings growth reached approximately **30%** (approx., verify before merging), well above long-run averages. However, companies beat consensus estimates by only **1.9%** on average, against a five-year norm of **7.5%**, signalling that elevated expectations had already been priced into valuations entering the season and limiting upside surprise as a positive catalyst.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equity markets in October were defined by the tension between strong aggregate earnings growth and a sharp deterioration in sentiment toward the AI infrastructure trade. Blended S&P 500 Q3 earnings growth came in at approximately **30%** year-on-year (approx., verify before merging), reflecting sustained top-line momentum from both enterprise technology and cyclical sectors. Yet companies beat consensus estimates by only **1.9%** — well below the five-year average beat rate of **7.5%** — signalling that expectations had been set too aggressively ahead of the season.

The Alphabet Q3 report on October 28 was the pivotal event: negative free cash flow of negative **$9.07 billion**, the company's first top-and-bottom-line miss in nearly four years, and **$51.36 billion** in quarterly capex crystallised investor anxiety over the near-term cash economics of the AI buildout. Shares fell more than **12%** in the following sessions, dragging the Nasdaq Composite down **5.28%** for the month — its steepest decline since March 2025. The technology sector ETF XLK shed **8.3%**, with broader AI hardware and semiconductor names compounding the losses.

In contrast, the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained **1.76%** as defensive sectors — healthcare, financials, consumer staples, and energy — absorbed substantial rotational inflows. The S&P 500 finished the month at approximately **-0.87%**, with an estimated close near **7,585** (approx., verify before merging). The Federal Reserve's October 28 decision to hold the target rate at **3.75%–4.00%** — with two hawkish dissents favouring an immediate hike — reinforced the view that monetary policy will remain restrictive for longer than equity markets had priced through mid-year, capping any recovery in rate-sensitive growth valuations.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities delivered a broadly constructive performance in October, with the region's structurally higher weighting in energy, financial, and pharmaceutical stocks insulating benchmarks from the worst of the US tech-driven derisking. The FTSE 100 rose approximately **+1%** to close near **10,730** (approx., verify before merging), marking its first monthly gain in three consecutive months and reflecting strength in AstraZeneca and energy majors lifted by the Brent crude rally. It was a clear case of sector composition trumping macro headwinds.

The DAX closed October 30 near **25,818** (approx., verify before merging) while the CAC 40 settled around **7,969** (approx., verify before merging). Both indices drew support from resilient industrial order data and ongoing restructuring in the European auto sector, though technology-adjacent components faced sympathy selling from the US derisking wave. The European Central Bank's data-dependent, comparatively dovish posture left investors less concerned about near-term policy tightening than their US counterparts, providing a modest valuation cushion to European growth stocks relative to their American peers.

Energy was the standout sector in absolute terms across the region: European majors rallied sharply as Brent surged toward **$118/bbl** on Hormuz supply-chain anxieties, boosting fourth-quarter free cash flow expectations materially. The divergence between the FTSE 100's energy and financial-heavy composition and the more growth-oriented CAC 40 meant UK equities outperformed their Continental peers on a risk-adjusted basis through most of the month, though both markets closed October ahead of their September levels.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asia-Pacific equity markets experienced a highly differentiated October, with Chinese mainland indices under acute pressure from AI hardware sector liquidation while regional markets with energy and financial exposure found footing. The Shanghai Composite fell approximately **6.3%** over the month, closing near **3,599** on October 30 (approx., verify before merging) — a fresh 52-week low — as ChiNext-listed AI hardware names, including optical-module and high-bandwidth memory chipmakers, saw aggressive selling amid concerns over AI capex sustainability globally. Year-to-date the index was down approximately **9.3%** (approx., verify before merging).

The Hang Seng demonstrated relative resilience, closing October 30 near **23,294** (approx., verify before merging). Investors rotated away from mainland Chinese technology into Hong Kong-listed consumer, logistics, and banking names, supported by strong mid-month trade data. State-backed buying on the mainland cushioned the Shanghai Composite from an even steeper decline, with record highs in state-owned bank stocks partially offsetting the AI hardware rout. The PBoC held its Loan Prime Rate steady, providing a stable backdrop but limiting the upside for rate-sensitive sectors.

In Japan, the Nikkei 225 closed October 30 at approximately **63,290** (approx., verify before merging), weighed by technology sector weakness and a strengthening yen impacting export earners. Domestic financial and energy stocks partially offset the decline, and ongoing Tokyo Stock Exchange-driven corporate governance reforms — pushing companies to improve capital efficiency and boost dividends — continued to attract medium-term institutional interest in Japanese equities despite the month's headwinds.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar staged a broad-based recovery in October, underpinned by the Federal Reserve's hawkish hold at **3.75%–4.00%** and the resurgence in US Treasury yields toward the **5%** mark. The DXY dollar index firmed to close near **102** (approx., verify before merging), extending gains from the **101.45** September close, as the yield differential argument reasserted itself with renewed conviction against major peers following the FOMC's hawkish October meeting minutes.

EUR/USD retreated to close the month at **1.1206**, reflecting the ECB's comparatively dovish posture and softer Eurozone growth indicators. GBP/USD ended October at **1.3397**, with sterling facing dual headwinds from US dollar strength and uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England's pace of easing following mixed UK labour market data. USD/JPY continued to grind higher, closing at **157.56**, as the yen remained under structural pressure from the persistent and wide US-Japan rate differential; the Bank of Japan's cautious normalisation pace offered limited resistance against the dollar's renewed firmness.

Emerging market currencies broadly weakened against the dollar over the month as higher US yields, elevated oil import costs, and risk-off sentiment in technology created a challenging macro trifecta. The oil price surge offered partial insulation for commodity-linked EM currencies — particularly in the Gulf and Latin America — but the net effect across the broader EM FX complex was negative, reinforcing a defensive posture heading into the final quarter of 2026.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Energy dominated commodity market narratives in October as Brent crude surged to a six-month high near **$118/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) by late month, driven by escalating attacks on tanker shipping near the Strait of Hormuz. Monthly gains of approximately **14%** for Brent made it the strongest-performing major commodity asset class of October. WTI crude settled near **$104/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) on October 30, with the Brent-WTI spread widening materially as logistics constraints and regional refinery demand patterns diverged. The pre-war strait had accounted for roughly one-fifth of global seaborne oil supply, and sustained disruption embedded a substantial risk premium across the entire energy complex.

Gold's performance was the month's most striking reversal. Spot gold fell approximately **6.5%** over October, closing near **$4,017** (approx., verify before merging) — at or near its one-year low — as the surge in US real yields and a firmer dollar eroded the metal's appeal as a store of value. The decline was the sharpest monthly loss of 2026 for gold, reversing much of the year's accumulated safe-haven premium as investors reassessed the inflation and growth outlook in light of the Fed's hawkish hold. Six major institutional houses subsequently revised their year-end gold price targets lower following the October sell-off.

Copper ended October down approximately **1.9%** on the London Metal Exchange, closing near **$14,130/tonne** (approx., verify before merging). The retreat reflected investor concern that AI data-centre capex trajectories — particularly following Alphabet's negative FCF print — could soften near-term demand for the metal in power and cooling infrastructure projects. Nonetheless, the medium-term structural case for copper remained intact given electrification, grid expansion, and EV adoption demand, limiting the month's decline to a relatively modest correction.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
October 2026 was a defining month for US fixed income, characterised by a volatile ratchet higher in yields driven by the Federal Reserve's hawkish policy hold and persistent inflationary signals from the energy complex. The 10-year US Treasury yield scaled a cycle high near **5.13%** in mid-October before retracing to close the month near **4.94%** (approx., verify before merging) — a material increase from the September close — while the 2-year yield reached an intra-month peak near **4.81%** before settling near **4.69%** (approx., verify before merging) by October 23.

The FOMC's October 28 vote to hold at **3.75%–4.00%** with two hawkish dissents reinforced the perception that the next policy move is as likely to be a hike as a cut, shifting terminal rate expectations materially higher. This recalibration of forward guidance, combined with elevated oil prices feeding into inflation breakevens, sustained pressure on the long end of the curve. Notably, October 22 saw the strongest single-session rally in US Treasuries in over a year, as a momentary flight-to-quality impulse triggered by risk-asset volatility around the Alphabet earnings event snapped yields sharply lower intraday before they resumed their upward trajectory.

The yield curve maintained a modestly positive slope, with the 10-year–2-year spread around **30–32 basis points** (approx., verify before merging), signalling that markets are not pricing an imminent recession but are increasingly uncertain about the growth-inflation policy trade-off heading into 2027. Rising yields weighed on credit spreads at the margin, with investment-grade spreads widening slightly over the month as the higher-for-longer narrative gained traction among fixed income investors globally.
